questions.prompt: In a transformer architecture, what does self-attention actually compute for each token?
options: A query for that token is compared against every other token's key to produce weighted relevance scores, which then blend their value vectors into a new, context-aware representation
A fixed dictionary lookup that maps each token directly to one predefined meaning
A running summary of the sequence so far, carried forward one word at a time
A classification of the token's part of speech, used only for grammar correction
A hash of the token's position in the sequence, used to compress the input
A separate neural network that translates the token into a different language before processing
questions.explain: Self-attention computes a query for each token and compares it against every other token's key to get relevance weights, then blends the corresponding value vectors into a new, context-aware representation — the mechanism that lets 'it' attend directly to 'cat' no matter how far apart they are in the sequence.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C describes how an older RNN works — carrying one running summary forward word by word — which is exactly the slow, long-range-forgetting approach transformers replaced. Self-attention instead lets every token connect directly to every other token at once, regardless of distance.

questions.prompt: In the sentence 'The cat sat because it was tired,' why does self-attention need 'it' to attend strongly to 'cat' specifically?
options: Because resolving what a pronoun refers to requires a direct, weighted connection to the correct earlier token, regardless of how many words separate them
Because 'cat' is the first word in the sentence, and attention always weights the first token most heavily
Because 'it' and 'cat' are adjacent in the model's vocabulary list
Because the sentence would fail to tokenize correctly otherwise
questions.explain: Self-attention gives every token a direct, weighted link to every other token, so 'it' can form a strong connection to 'cat' specifically — producing a context-aware representation of 'it' that effectively means 'it (the cat)' — regardless of the distance between the two words.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about why modern LLMs use subword tokenization (like Byte-Pair Encoding) instead of a whole-word vocabulary.
options: A closed whole-word vocabulary will eventually hit a word it has never seen, such as a typo or brand name
Subword tokenization gives the model a fixed-size vocabulary that can still represent literally any string, falling back to individual bytes if needed
Frequent whole words still get their own single token under subword tokenization
Subword tokenization guarantees exactly one token per English word, with no exceptions
The English language has too few words for a whole-word vocabulary to be practical
questions.explain: English alone has hundreds of thousands of words, so any closed whole-word vocabulary eventually fails on something unseen. Subword tokenization solves this with a fixed vocabulary of common chunks — frequent words get one token, rarer words split into pieces, and in the worst case it can fall back to individual bytes, so it can represent any string.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: as a rough rule of thumb for English text, a token represents about ________ of a word (or equivalently, about 100 tokens for every 75 words of plain English).
questions.explain: The guide's rule of thumb is roughly 0.75 words per token for English — an approximation that shifts by model and content, not a fixed law.

questions.prompt: Match each embeddings-related term to its correct meaning.
right: Searching by meaning via embeddings instead of exact keyword matching
A vector of numbers representing a token's or text's meaning
The high-dimensional space where distance between embeddings encodes meaning
A measure of how close two embeddings are, based on the angle between them
questions.explain: Embedding is the meaning-vector itself; cosine similarity measures closeness by angle; semantic search is searching by meaning via embeddings; vector space is the high-dimensional space where that distance lives.

questions.prompt: Why does an LLM re-process the entire sequence so far for every single token it generates, instead of just picking up where it left off?
options: Because autoregressive generation means each new token depends on everything generated so far, including tokens the model itself just produced, so the full context has to be re-read each step
Because the model has a hard limit of one token per API call and must restart the connection each time
Because tokenization has to be redone from scratch for every new token
Because the model caches nothing and intentionally forgets the system prompt after the first token
questions.explain: Autoregressive generation appends each chosen token to the sequence and runs the whole process again, now predicting the next token after that — so every token, including ones the model just generated itself, is part of the context for the next prediction.

questions.prompt: Put the four stages of the transformer pipeline in the order text actually moves through them, from raw input to a generated reply.
items: Tokenize — break the input text into tokens
Embed — convert each token into a vector encoding meaning
Attend — let every token weigh which others matter to it
Predict — turn the result into a probability distribution over the next token
questions.explain: Every transformer-based LLM moves text through these four stages in order: tokenize, embed, attend (self-attention), then predict a probability distribution over the next token.

questions.prompt: Why is hallucination described as a predictable consequence of next-token prediction, rather than a separate, unrelated bug?
options: Because the model's generation mechanism only optimizes for producing a probable next token, with no built-in check for whether that token is actually true
Because hallucination only happens when the model's training data contains factual errors
Because hallucination is a random hardware fault that occurs independently of how the model generates text
Because every model is deliberately trained to occasionally produce false statements for variety
questions.explain: Next-token prediction optimizes purely for plausibility, not truth. When training patterns are strong, probable and true usually line up — but nothing in the mechanism separately verifies truth, so confident, fluent, wrong output (hallucination) is a direct consequence of how generation works, not a bolted-on flaw.

questions.prompt: Select every condition that reliably increases the chance of an LLM hallucinating, per the lesson.
options: Asking for a precise citation or exact statistic the model has to generate from a general pattern rather than a memorized fact
A topic with thin training coverage, such as a niche subject or a very recent event
A leading or loaded prompt that assumes a false premise
A long, multi-step generation where an early small error can compound
Asking the model a simple, well-documented, widely discussed factual question
questions.explain: Specificity without grounding, thin training coverage, leading/loaded prompts, and long multi-step generations where an early error compounds are the four conditions the lesson calls out as reliably increasing hallucination risk. A simple, well-documented question is the opposite case — where probable and true usually line up.

questions.prompt: What is the key distinction between an 'open-weight' model and a 'closed' model?
options: Open-weight models distribute their trained weights for download under a license, while closed models are accessible only through a hosted API with no weights distributed
Open-weight models are always free of charge, while closed models always require payment
Open-weight models are smaller in parameter count than closed models by definition
Closed models can be fine-tuned, while open-weight models cannot be fine-tuned at all
Open-weight models are only available for image generation, not text
Closed models publish their full training data, while open-weight models never do
questions.explain: The real distinction is access to the trained weights themselves: open-weight models (like Llama 4) let you download the weights under a license, while closed models (like Claude, GPT) are API-only — you never receive the weights.
questions.distractorExplain: Option F is backwards — closed models like Claude and GPT never publish their training data or their weights, and open-weight models like Llama typically don't publish their original training data either. 'Open-weight' refers specifically to the trained weights being downloadable, not the training data or training code.

questions.prompt: Per Anthropic's own tier descriptions, which Claude model is positioned for 'long-running agentic coding and knowledge work'?
options: Claude Opus 5.5
Claude Haiku 4.5
Claude Sonnet 5.5
Claude Fable 5.1
questions.explain: Anthropic's own documentation describes Claude Opus 5.5 specifically as being for 'long-running agentic coding and knowledge work,' sitting above Sonnet 5.5 (the speed/intelligence balance tier) and below Fable 5.1 (reserved for the most demanding reasoning).

questions.prompt: A team is building a high-volume, low-complexity FAQ chatbot with tight latency expectations. Which starting strategy from the lesson's worked example fits best?
options: Efficiency-first: start with the fastest/cheapest tier, test thoroughly, and upgrade only if testing reveals a real capability gap
Capability-first: start with the flagship tier and look for room to downgrade later
Skip model selection entirely and let the end user pick the model
Always use the same model tier used for the multi-step coding agent example
questions.explain: The lesson's worked example maps a high-volume, low-complexity, latency-sensitive FAQ chatbot to the efficiency-first strategy: start with the fastest/cheapest tier and only upgrade where real testing shows a genuine capability gap.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the real trade-offs between open-weight and closed models.
options: Closed models give you a managed, continuously-updated service with no infrastructure to run
Open-weight models let you self-host, fine-tune without external approval, and inspect what you're running
Open-weight models shift the operational burden of running and scaling GPUs onto you
Closed models let you download the full trained weights for your own servers
There is no real trade-off — open-weight models are strictly better in every case
questions.explain: Closed models trade convenience (managed, scaling, continuously updated) for never giving you the weights. Open-weight models trade that convenience back for control (self-hosting, fine-tuning without approval, auditability) at the cost of owning your own infrastructure burden.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Anthropic's published deprecation policy, Anthropic commits to at least ________ days' notice before retiring a publicly released model.
questions.explain: Anthropic commits to at least 60 days' notice before retiring a publicly released model — the real Claude Sonnet 4.5 deprecation case in the lesson gave 61 days, just over that minimum.

questions.prompt: Match each company to its current model family.
right: GPT
Grok
Claude
Gemini
questions.explain: Anthropic's family is Claude, OpenAI's is GPT, Google's is Gemini, and xAI's is Grok.

questions.prompt: In a request to Anthropic's Messages API, which two fields are strictly required?
options: `model` and `max_tokens`
`model` and `system`
`messages` and `temperature`
`stream` and `tools`
`system` and `stream`
`max_tokens` and `tool_choice`
questions.explain: Only `model` (which model answers) and `max_tokens` (the hard cap on reply length) are required on a Messages API request, alongside a populated `messages` array. `system`, sampling parameters, `stream`, and `tools` are all optional.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B is wrong because `system` is optional, not required — a request can omit it entirely and still succeed with just `model`, `max_tokens`, and a `messages` array.

questions.prompt: A developer ports working Anthropic Messages API code to OpenAI's Chat Completions API and the system prompt silently stops applying. What's the most likely cause?
options: Anthropic treats `system` as a separate top-level field, while OpenAI expects it as a `system`-role entry inside the `messages` array
OpenAI's API doesn't support system prompts at all
System prompts only work when `stream` is set to `false`
The `max_tokens` field must be removed before a system prompt will apply
questions.explain: Anthropic's Messages API puts `system` as its own top-level request field, outside `messages`. OpenAI's Chat Completions API instead puts it inside the `messages` array as a `system`-role entry. Porting code without accounting for that shape difference means the instructions either get silently dropped or rejected.

questions.prompt: On Claude models released after Opus 4.6, what happens if you send a `temperature` value other than 1.0?
options: The request is rejected — only 1.0 is still accepted, for backwards compatibility, because `temperature` is deprecated on these models
The value is silently clamped to the nearest valid number between 0 and 2
It's accepted normally and reshapes the output distribution as it always has
It's ignored with no error, and the model falls back to `top_p` automatically
questions.explain: Anthropic's current Messages API reference states that models released after Claude Opus 4.6 no longer support tuning `temperature` — a value of 1.0 is accepted for backwards compatibility, but any other value is rejected outright. `top_p` and `top_k` remain the live sampling controls on current models.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about tool/function calling in Anthropic's Messages API.
options: The model never executes the tool itself — it only replies with a structured request naming the tool and arguments
A `tool_result` block must reference the exact `tool_use_id` of the tool call it's answering
The `input` on a `tool_use` block is already a parsed object matching your schema, not a string you parse yourself
Setting `tool_choice` to `{"type": "none"}` forces the model to call some tool
`disable_parallel_tool_use: true` allows the model to call more tools per turn, not fewer
questions.explain: The model only requests a tool call — your code executes it. The `tool_result` you send back must reference the original `tool_use_id`, and the `input` on a `tool_use` block arrives already parsed. `{"type": "none"}` actually forbids any tool call, and `disable_parallel_tool_use: true` restricts the model to at most one tool call per turn, not more.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Anthropic's streaming event sequence when `stream: true` is set.
options: `message_start` arrives first, with an empty `content` array
`content_block_delta` events carry the incremental text fragments
A `ping` event is a safe-to-ignore keep-alive with no meaningful data
`message_delta` carries the final `stop_reason` and completed `usage` counts
The stream ends with a literal `[DONE]` sentinel, the same as OpenAI's streaming format
questions.explain: Anthropic's real event sequence starts with `message_start`, carries text via `content_block_delta`, may include a safely-ignorable `ping`, and reports final `stop_reason`/`usage` in `message_delta` before `message_stop`. The literal `[DONE]` sentinel is OpenAI's convention, not Anthropic's — Anthropic ends with a `message_stop` event instead.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: if a Messages API response comes back with `stop_reason` set to `________`, that means the reply was cut off before finishing, not that it reached a natural end.
questions.explain: `max_tokens` as a `stop_reason` means generation was cut off at your token limit — an incomplete reply your application should treat differently from `end_turn`, which means the model reached a natural stopping point.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Anthropic's current dedicated structured-output feature is configured through a request field called ________, which constrains the model's output during generation to match a JSON Schema.
questions.explain: `output_config.format` carries a JSON Schema that constrains generation token-by-token so the result is guaranteed to validate — not just checked after the fact — distinguishing it from simply asking in plain English for 'only JSON.'

questions.prompt: Match each `stop_reason` value to what it means.
right: The model is pausing to let your application run a tool
The model reached a natural stopping point
The model declined to produce schema-conforming output
Generation was cut off at your token limit
questions.explain: end_turn means a natural stop; max_tokens means the reply was cut off; tool_use means the model is pausing for a tool call; refusal means the model declined to produce schema-conforming output.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of an LLM API request's lifecycle in the order they actually happen, from your code to the model and back.
items: Build the request — assemble the JSON body
Authenticate — the request carries real API-key headers
Validate — the API checks the request shape before any model work happens
Tokenize — your text is converted into token IDs
Generate — the model runs inference, producing tokens one at a time
Return or stream — the reply comes back all at once or incrementally
Bill & log — usage is attached to the response and a request-id is logged
questions.explain: The real request journey is: build the request, authenticate, validate the shape, tokenize the text, generate tokens, return or stream the reply, then bill and log the usage — the whole chapter's lessons map onto different steps of this one journey.

questions.prompt: Which of these is specifically called out in the lesson as NOT a good reason to fine-tune a model?
options: The model doesn't know a recent fact — this is usually better solved with retrieval (RAG), not fine-tuning
A narrow, repeated output style that's hard to describe in words but easy to show with examples
Shrinking a long, repeated system prompt into the model's weights to cut recurring per-call token cost
A latency-sensitive, narrow task where a smaller fine-tuned model could match a bigger model's quality
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly calls out that 'the model doesn't know a fact' is not a fine-tuning problem — that's what retrieval (RAG) is for. Fine-tuning tends to memorize specific examples rather than reliably generalizing new factual knowledge, making it a poor, expensive substitute for grounding a model in real documents at request time.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation).
options: The original model weights are frozen entirely and never updated
Only small, newly-inserted low-rank matrices are trained
A trained LoRA adapter can optionally be merged back into the base weights for zero extra inference latency
LoRA requires updating every weight in the model, the same as a full fine-tune
Because the base model is shared and frozen, different LoRA adapters can be swapped on top of it like plugins
questions.explain: LoRA freezes the original weights entirely and trains only small inserted low-rank matrices (often under 1% of the full model's parameters), which can be merged back into the base weights at zero extra inference cost, and swapped like plugins since the shared base model never changes. A full fine-tune, by contrast, updates every weight — which is exactly what LoRA avoids.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: LoRA stands for ________.
questions.explain: LoRA stands for Low-Rank Adaptation — freezing the base model's weights and training small, low-rank matrices as a learned 'detour' instead of updating the full weight matrices.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a fine-tuning job's training compute cost is actually billed based on ________, the total tokens the training run consumed (data size times epochs).
questions.explain: OpenAI's fine-tuning jobs bill based on `trained_tokens` — not a flat fee or a per-example charge — which is exactly why epoch count and dataset size directly drive training cost.

questions.prompt: Match each fine-tuning cost component to its description.
right: A fine-tuned model is typically more expensive to call per token than the base model it was built from
Usually the single largest cost in the project, even though it never appears on a provider's pricing page
A full fine-tune produces a complete model-sized artifact that must be stored and served
When the underlying base model is retired, the fine-tune must be retrained from scratch on the new base
questions.explain: Data collection is usually the largest, least-visible cost; the inference surcharge makes a fine-tuned model typically more expensive per call than its base; storage/hosting means a full fine-tune's artifact must be stored and served at full model size; and base model deprecation forces a full retrain whenever the underlying model is retired.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of a self-serve fine-tuning job in the order they actually happen.
items: Prepare labeled training examples
Upload the training file and get back a file ID
Create the fine-tuning job referencing that file
Wait while the job trains
Receive a new fine-tuned model ID once it succeeds
Call the new model ID like any other chat completion model
questions.explain: The mechanical flow is: prepare examples, upload the file, create the job, let it train, get back a new model ID, then call that model ID exactly like any other chat completion model.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of properly evaluating a fine-tuned model in the correct order.
items: Set aside a held-out evaluation set before training begins
Train the fine-tuned model without ever exposing it to the held-out set
Run the same held-out prompts through both the base and fine-tuned model
Check a regression suite on unrelated tasks for catastrophic forgetting
questions.explain: A real evaluation sets aside held-out data before training, trains without touching that data, then compares the base and fine-tuned model on the same held-out prompts, and finally checks an unrelated-task regression suite — the step most teams skip — to catch catastrophic forgetting.

questions.prompt: Why can't Claude be used to generate a new image from a text prompt?
options: Per Anthropic's own documentation, Claude is an image understanding model only — it cannot generate, produce, edit, or create images
Claude can generate images, but only through a separate, undocumented API endpoint
Image generation requires a diffusion model, and all of Claude's models use the transformer architecture instead
Claude's context window is too small to support any image-related task
questions.explain: Anthropic's own documentation states Claude is 'an image understanding model only... it cannot generate, produce, edit, manipulate, or create images.' Understanding an image and generating one are different capabilities, and Claude only has the first — an application that needs both has to pair Claude with a separate image-generation provider like OpenAI's GPT Image 2.5 or Google's Nano Banana.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the documented limitations of current vision-language models.
options: Accuracy drops on low-quality, rotated, or very small (under roughly 200px) images
Object counting is approximate, not exact, especially with many small objects
Spatial or coordinate output is approximate, not pixel-perfect
No current vision model should be trusted to reliably detect whether an image itself was AI-generated
Current vision-language models can reliably identify specific named individuals in a photo
questions.explain: Per Anthropic's own documented limitations, vision models struggle with low-quality/rotated/tiny images, give only approximate counts and spatial coordinates, and cannot reliably detect whether an image is AI-generated. They also cannot reliably identify specific people — the opposite of the last option's claim.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Claude breaks an image into ________-pixel patches, and each patch costs one visual token.
questions.explain: Claude divides an image into 28×28-pixel patches, with each patch costing one visual token — which is why a 1920×1080 screenshot can cost roughly 1,500–2,700 visual tokens depending on the model's resolution tier.

questions.prompt: Match each audio/voice capability to its definition.
right: A product built around native (or chained) speech-to-speech interaction
Audio in, a text transcript out
Audio in, audio out, without a required text intermediate step
Text in, synthesized audio out
questions.explain: STT converts audio to a text transcript; TTS converts text to synthesized audio; native speech-to-speech goes audio-to-audio without a required text step in between; and a voice agent is the product built around that (or a chained) speech interaction.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of how a diffusion-based image generator produces an image in the correct order.
items: Begin from pure random noise
Iteratively denoise the image over multiple steps, guided by the prompt
Arrive at a final, coherent image matching the prompt
questions.explain: A diffusion model like GPT Image 2.5 or Nano Banana starts from random noise and repeatedly refines it, step by step, into a coherent image guided by the prompt — like a sculptor removing material until a shape emerges, rather than predicting the image piece by piece the way an autoregressive model does.

questions.prompt: In the capstone's conversation loop, why must the assistant's full streamed reply be manually appended back onto the `messages` list after streaming finishes?
options: Because the SDK's streaming wrapper doesn't do that for you, and without it the next API call won't include that turn — the model will appear to 'forget' it
Because `messages` resets itself automatically after every streamed response
Because the Messages API stores conversation history server-side and `messages` is only used for the first turn
Because `system` and `messages` must always contain identical content
questions.explain: `client.messages.stream(...)` yields incremental text fragments, but it never appends anything to your `messages` list for you. Skipping the manual `messages.append(...)` after streaming finishes means that turn never makes it into history, so the model loses access to it on the next call — demonstrating Lesson 4's point that the model has no memory beyond what's resent in `messages`.

questions.prompt: Select every requirement the capstone's rubric actually states for the finished chat application.
options: It maintains a growing `messages` list across turns, not just one message
It uses `stream: true` so replies print incrementally, not all at once
It includes a system prompt that gives the assistant a defined persona or purpose
It lets the user type `quit` (or similar) to exit cleanly
It must use function/tool calling as a required core feature
questions.explain: The Lesson 29 rubric lists exactly four requirements: a growing `messages` list, `stream: true` for incremental output, a system prompt with a defined persona, and a clean way to quit. Tool calling, structured output, and image input are optional later extensions, not core rubric requirements.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the capstone's Python build calls Anthropic's streaming endpoint through the SDK method ________, used as a context manager whose `.text_stream` attribute is iterated to print each fragment as it arrives.
questions.explain: `client.messages.stream(...)` is the SDK's higher-level context-manager wrapper around the raw server-sent events from Lesson 16 — iterating `stream.text_stream` yields each text fragment without you ever having to parse raw SSE events yourself.

questions.prompt: Match each chapter of the course to what it specifically gave the final capstone build, per the course's own closing recap.
right: The exact request/response/streaming shapes the build runs on
Why a system prompt, not a fine-tune, was the right tool for persona
Why `messages` has to carry the full history every single turn
How to choose and justify a specific model for the build
questions.explain: Chapter 1 explains why `messages` must carry full history every turn (no model memory between calls); Chapter 2 is how you pick and justify a model; Chapter 3 supplies the exact request/response/streaming shapes the build uses; and Chapter 4 explains why a system prompt, not a fine-tune, was the right tool here.
